brazil/arpoador.name: Arpoador sunset viewpoint
brazil/arpoador.description: A rocky point between Copacabana and Ipanema beaches where surfers and crowds gather to watch the sunset.
brazil/arpoador.details: Arpoador sits on the small headland that separates Copacabana from Ipanema, and its flat rocks fill with people most evenings as the sun sets over the hills behind the city. Surfers use the point break just offshore through the day, and the crowd thins out again shortly after dark. It is an easy, flat walk from either beach. Arrive with some time to spare, since the best rocks fill up first.

brazil/ipanema-dinner.name: Dinner in Ipanema
brazil/ipanema-dinner.description: A sit-down dinner in one of Ipanema's many restaurants, from simple grilled fish to a full Brazilian menu.

brazil/christ-the-redeemer.name: Christ the Redeemer
brazil/christ-the-redeemer.description: An Art Deco statue on the summit of Corcovado mountain, overlooking the whole of Rio de Janeiro.
brazil/christ-the-redeemer.details: The statue stands on Corcovado, one of the granite peaks that rise directly from the city, and is reached by a cog train, a van, or a short hike from the upper station. Clouds often roll in over the mountain by the middle of the day, so a morning visit gives the best chance of a clear view both of the statue and of the city spread out below. The platform around the statue's base gets crowded at peak times. It is one of the most recognisable monuments in the Americas.

brazil/santa-teresa.name: Santa Teresa and Parque das Ruínas
brazil/santa-teresa.description: A hillside neighbourhood of cobbled lanes and old mansions, including a ruined mansion turned into a public viewpoint.
brazil/santa-teresa.details: Santa Teresa grew up on a steep hill above the centre as a retreat for Rio's wealthier residents in the 19th century, and much of its winding street layout and older architecture survives. Parque das Ruínas preserves the shell of one such mansion, with modern walkways built through the ruin and a rooftop terrace looking back across the city toward Corcovado and Sugarloaf. The streets are steep and sometimes cobbled, so comfortable shoes help. A yellow tram line once served the neighbourhood and still runs on a limited route.

brazil/lapa-samba.name: Samba night in Lapa
brazil/lapa-samba.description: An evening of live samba music in one of the bars and clubs beneath Lapa's old aqueduct.
brazil/lapa-samba.details: Lapa sits below the Arcos da Lapa, a tall colonial-era aqueduct that now frames the neighbourhood's nightlife district, and its streets fill with bars, samba clubs and street vendors most evenings. Several venues host live samba and choro bands, with dancing expected rather than optional in some rooms. The area is busy and reasonably well lit on the main streets, though it is sensible to keep valuables close and stick to the livelier blocks. Weekends are noticeably busier than weekdays.

brazil/sugarloaf.name: Sugarloaf Mountain cable car
brazil/sugarloaf.description: A two-stage cable car ride to the summit of a granite peak at the entrance to Guanabara Bay.
brazil/sugarloaf.details: The cable car climbs in two stages, first to Morro da Urca and then on to the summit of Pão de Açúcar, a bare granite dome at the mouth of Guanabara Bay. The top gives a wide view that takes in the bay, the airport runway, and the beach neighbourhoods curving away to the south. Sunset is the most popular time to go, so the cars and platforms are busiest then. Each stage is a separate short ride, with an open viewing area at the middle station as well as the summit.

brazil/urca-seawall.name: Urca seawall stroll
brazil/urca-seawall.description: A flat waterfront path in the quiet Urca neighbourhood, looking back across the bay toward Sugarloaf.
brazil/urca-seawall.details: Urca is a small, low-rise neighbourhood at the foot of Sugarloaf, far calmer than the beach districts further south. A seawall path runs along its edge, used by local families and runners rather than tour groups, with views back across Guanabara Bay. There is no beach here in the usual sense, just the wall and a narrow strip of sand exposed at low tide. It pairs naturally with a Sugarloaf cable car visit, since the cable car station is a short walk away.

brazil/ipanema-beach.name: Afternoon at Ipanema Beach
brazil/ipanema-beach.description: One of Rio's best-known city beaches, backed by apartment towers and divided into numbered sections called postos.
brazil/ipanema-beach.details: Ipanema runs along the coast between two of the city's granite outcrops, and its sand is organised into numbered posto sections, each with a slightly different crowd. Chair and umbrella rental, and vendors selling drinks and snacks, work the beach through the day. Lifeguard posts mark safer swimming areas, since currents can be strong in places. Sunset over the Dois Irmãos peaks at the beach's western end is a well-known daily sight.

brazil/botafogo-dinner.name: Dinner in Botafogo
brazil/botafogo-dinner.description: A dinner in Botafogo, a residential neighbourhood on the bay with a more local, less touristed restaurant scene.

brazil/rio-historic-centre.name: Rio historic centre walk
brazil/rio-historic-centre.description: The older downtown core of Rio, with colonial-era churches, early 20th-century theatres and narrow commercial streets.
brazil/rio-historic-centre.details: Rio's historic centre, known as Centro, holds the oldest layer of the city, including colonial churches, the ornate early 20th-century theatre and library buildings around Cinelândia, and a dense grid of commercial streets. It empties out in the evenings and on weekends once the office crowds leave, so a weekday visit shows it at its liveliest. The area is mostly flat and walkable, though some streets are narrow and crowded at midday. It gives a different picture of the city than the beach neighbourhoods.

brazil/tijuca-forest.name: Tijuca National Forest and Cascatinha Taunay
brazil/tijuca-forest.description: A large area of replanted rainforest inside the city limits, with trails, viewpoints and a waterfall.
brazil/tijuca-forest.details: Tijuca National Forest is one of the largest areas of urban forest in the world, largely replanted in the 19th century after the original cover had been cleared for coffee farms. Cascatinha Taunay, a modest waterfall near one of the park entrances, makes an easy first stop, with longer trails and viewpoints such as Vista Chinesa further in. The forest is noticeably cooler and quieter than the city below it. Paths are mostly shaded but can be uneven, and some sections are steep.

brazil/iguazu-falls-brazilian-side.name: Iguaçu National Park, Brazilian side
brazil/iguazu-falls-brazilian-side.description: A walkway along the canyon rim on the Brazilian side of the Iguazu Falls, ending at a close-up platform below the main cascades.
brazil/iguazu-falls-brazilian-side.details: The Brazilian side of the falls is the shorter of the two national parks but gives the wider panoramic view, since the walkway runs along the canyon rim facing the horseshoe of falls on the Argentine side. A shuttle bus from the entrance leads to the start of the trail, which ends at a platform and a glass elevator close to one of the main cascades, where the spray is constant. Rain ponchos are worth having near the platform even on a dry day. The whole walk, including the bus ride, takes a few hours at an easy pace.

brazil/parque-das-aves.name: Parque das Aves (Bird Park)
brazil/parque-das-aves.description: A series of large walk-through aviaries beside the Iguaçu National Park entrance, home to toucans, macaws and other birds native to the region.
brazil/parque-das-aves.details: Parque das Aves sits right beside the entrance to the Brazilian national park, so it combines easily with a falls visit on the same day. Several large, planted aviaries let visitors walk among free-flying birds rather than view them from outside a cage, including toucans and macaws native to the surrounding forest. Paths are flat and shaded, and the visit typically takes a couple of hours. It is a straightforward way to see species that are otherwise easy to miss in the wild.

brazil/itaipu-dam.name: Itaipu Dam
brazil/itaipu-dam.description: One of the world's largest hydroelectric dams, built on the river that forms part of the border between Brazil and Paraguay.
brazil/itaipu-dam.details: Itaipu was built jointly by Brazil and Paraguay on the Paraná River and remains one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants by output. A visitor centre on the Brazilian side runs guided tours that explain the scale of the structure and look out over the dam wall and reservoir. The standard tour covers the exterior and viewpoints rather than the working turbine halls. It makes a half-day outing that pairs naturally with a visit to the falls on the same trip.

brazil/avenida-paulista.name: Avenida Paulista and MASP
brazil/avenida-paulista.description: São Paulo's best-known avenue, lined with skyscrapers and home to the São Paulo Museum of Art's distinctive elevated gallery building.
brazil/avenida-paulista.details: Avenida Paulista runs through the heart of São Paulo and is closed to cars on Sundays, when it fills with cyclists, street performers and market stalls. The São Paulo Museum of Art, known as MASP, stands out for its concrete building raised on tall red pillars above an open ground-floor plaza. Inside, the collection spans European and Brazilian painting displayed on glass easels rather than walls. The avenue is flat and easy walking, lined with cafes for a break.

brazil/sao-paulo-dinner.name: Dinner in São Paulo
brazil/sao-paulo-dinner.description: A dinner reflecting São Paulo's reputation as Brazil's food capital, from a traditional churrascaria to the city's large Italian and Japanese-influenced scenes.

brazil/sao-paulo-historic-centre.name: São Paulo historic centre walk
brazil/sao-paulo-historic-centre.description: The older downtown core of São Paulo, denser and less manicured than the newer business districts further south.
brazil/sao-paulo-historic-centre.details: São Paulo's historic centre holds the city's oldest surviving buildings alongside early 20th-century towers such as the Edifício Martinelli, once South America's tallest building. The area is busy with office workers and street vendors by day and quieter, with more visible homelessness, after dark, so a daytime visit on the main streets is more comfortable. It is a useful contrast to the newer, wealthier neighbourhoods most visitors spend the rest of their time in. The streets are flat but can be crowded.

brazil/mercado-municipal.name: Mercado Municipal
brazil/mercado-municipal.description: A covered produce and food hall in central São Paulo, known for its stained-glass windows and oversized sandwiches.
brazil/mercado-municipal.details: The Mercado Municipal opened in the early 20th century as a wholesale produce market and is now better known for its food stalls, in particular a mortadella sandwich sold thick enough to need two hands. Stalls selling tropical fruit, dried goods and spices line the main hall beneath stained-glass windows depicting rural scenes. It gets busy around lunchtime, when queues form at the best-known counters. The building itself is worth a slow look as well as the food.

brazil/vila-madalena.name: Vila Madalena street art walk
brazil/vila-madalena.description: A hilly São Paulo neighbourhood known for its dense street art, independent shops and bar scene.
brazil/vila-madalena.details: Vila Madalena built its reputation on the murals and graffiti that cover many of its walls, most famously along the steep Beco do Batman alley, which changes constantly as new artists paint over older work. By day the neighbourhood suits a slow walk between galleries, design shops and cafes; by night its bars draw a younger crowd. The streets are hilly, with some steep stretches between the main points of interest. It sits a short distance from the university district, which shapes its creative, slightly bohemian character.

brazil/marco-tres-fronteiras.name: Marco das Três Fronteiras
brazil/marco-tres-fronteiras.description: A lookout point in Foz do Iguaçu where Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet at the confluence of the Iguaçu and Paraná rivers.
brazil/marco-tres-fronteiras.details: The monument marks the point where the Iguaçu River joins the much larger Paraná River, with Argentina visible across one channel and Paraguay across the other. Matching monuments stand on the Argentine and Paraguayan banks, each painted in that country's colours, and are easiest to make out with binoculars or a zoom lens. It is a brief stop rather than an attraction in its own right, often combined with the Itaipu Dam or a day otherwise spent at the falls. The viewing area is flat and paved.

brazil/pelourinho.name: Pelourinho colonial old town
brazil/pelourinho.description: Salvador's historic centre, a hillside quarter of brightly painted colonial buildings, churches and cobbled squares.
brazil/pelourinho.details: Pelourinho was the commercial heart of colonial Salvador and is now a UNESCO-listed collection of restored baroque churches, merchant houses and cobbled squares, many painted in strong colours. Live music and capoeira demonstrations spill into the streets through the day, especially around the main squares. The streets are steep and cobbled in places, which can be uneven underfoot. Most churches and museums close by early evening, so plan an afternoon visit if seeing the interiors matters.

brazil/capoeira-salvador.name: Capoeira demonstration and class
brazil/capoeira-salvador.description: An introduction to capoeira, the Afro-Brazilian martial art and dance form that developed in Bahia, with a demonstration and a beginner-friendly class.
brazil/capoeira-salvador.details: Capoeira combines dance, acrobatics and sparring movements set to call-and-response music played on a berimbau and drums, and it developed among enslaved and formerly enslaved communities in Bahia. Academies in Pelourinho offer short sessions for visitors that usually open with a demonstration before a simple class in footwork and basic movements. No experience or particular fitness level is assumed for a beginner class. Loose, comfortable clothing works best, and most sessions are done barefoot or in light shoes.

brazil/mercado-modelo.name: Mercado Modelo
brazil/mercado-modelo.description: A former customs house on Salvador's waterfront, now a market of stalls selling Bahian crafts, art and musical instruments.
brazil/mercado-modelo.details: The building served as a customs house in the colonial period before being converted into a covered craft market, and its stalls now sell leatherwork, woodcarving, lace and the berimbaus and other instruments used in capoeira. It sits directly on the waterfront below the old town, with a lift and a set of stairs connecting the two levels of the city. Bargaining is common practice here. It makes an easy stop between the old town above and the ferry terminal below.

brazil/farol-da-barra.name: Farol da Barra sunset
brazil/farol-da-barra.description: A lighthouse and small fort at the point where Salvador's bay meets the open Atlantic, a well-known sunset spot.
brazil/farol-da-barra.details: The fort and lighthouse at Barra mark the point where the sheltered waters of the Bay of All Saints give way to the open ocean, a position that made it one of the city's earliest defensive points. A small maritime museum occupies part of the fort. Crowds gather along the surrounding seafront most evenings for the sunset, with vendors and informal music adding to the atmosphere. The area around the fort is flat and paved.

brazil/porto-da-barra-beach.name: Porto da Barra beach
brazil/porto-da-barra-beach.description: A sheltered city beach in Salvador, calmer than the open-ocean beaches further along the coast.
brazil/porto-da-barra-beach.details: Porto da Barra sits inside the bay rather than facing the open Atlantic, so its water is generally calmer than beaches further south along the coast. It is close to hotels and restaurants in the Barra neighbourhood, making it a convenient choice rather than the most dramatic stretch of sand in the city. Chair and umbrella rental and beach vendors are available through the day. It gets busy on weekends with a mostly local crowd.

brazil/bale-folclorico.name: Balé Folclórico da Bahia performance
brazil/bale-folclorico.description: A folk dance company's staged performance of capoeira, candomblé and other Afro-Brazilian traditions, set to live music.
brazil/bale-folclorico.details: The company draws on Afro-Brazilian religious and cultural traditions, including candomblé and capoeira, reworking them into a staged theatrical performance with live percussion. Performances run for a set length in a small theatre in Pelourinho, usually a single evening show. It gives a more structured, easier-to-follow introduction to traditions that are otherwise encountered informally in the street. Seating is general rather than assigned in most venues.

brazil/pantanal-sunset-boat.name: Sunset wildlife-watching boat ride
brazil/pantanal-sunset-boat.description: A gentle evening boat ride along a Pantanal river channel, watching caimans and birds settle in for the night.

brazil/pantanal-jeep-safari.name: Pantanal sunrise jeep safari
brazil/pantanal-jeep-safari.description: An open 4x4 drive through the Pantanal wetland at dawn, when capybaras, caimans and birdlife are most active.
brazil/pantanal-jeep-safari.details: The Pantanal is the world's largest tropical wetland, flooding seasonally across a vast area of central-western Brazil and supporting dense concentrations of wildlife along its waterways. An open-sided 4x4 covers unpaved tracks through the lodge's surrounding land, with a guide pointing out capybaras, caimans, deer and birdlife that are most visible in the cooler hours around dawn. Vehicles and sightings depend on the season, since water levels change which areas are accessible. A hat and sun protection are worth having even for an early start.

brazil/pantanal-canoe.name: Canoe trip and piranha fishing
brazil/pantanal-canoe.description: A guided canoe trip on a Pantanal waterway, with the option to fish for piranha from the boat.
brazil/pantanal-canoe.details: A guide paddles or poles the canoe along a quiet channel, pointing out caimans resting on the banks and birds working the shallows. Piranha fishing is usually included as an option, with the guide handling hooks and releasing the fish afterwards rather than keeping them. The pace is slow and the trip suits most fitness levels, though sitting in a canoe for an extended period is worth bearing in mind. Water levels and wildlife visible vary with the season.

brazil/pantanal-horseback.name: Horseback riding through the wetlands
brazil/pantanal-horseback.description: A horseback outing through the Pantanal at walking pace, a quieter way to approach grazing wildlife than a vehicle.
brazil/pantanal-horseback.details: Horses are a traditional way of getting around the Pantanal's ranches and still used by local cattle hands, so lodges generally keep a string of calm, experienced horses for guided visitor rides. Riding at a walking pace allows closer, quieter approaches to grazing capybaras and birds than a vehicle normally allows. Rides are usually suited to beginners as well as more experienced riders, though anyone unfamiliar with horses should say so beforehand. Conditions underfoot vary with how recently the land has flooded.

brazil/pantanal-night-safari.name: Night safari for caiman and nocturnal wildlife
brazil/pantanal-night-safari.description: A spotlight-led drive or boat trip after dark, when caiman eyes reflect red in the light and nocturnal species become active.
brazil/pantanal-night-safari.details: After dark, a guide uses a handheld spotlight to pick out the red eyeshine of caimans resting at the water's edge, along with nocturnal birds and mammals that stay hidden during the day. The outing runs by vehicle or boat depending on the lodge and the water level at the time. It is a quieter, slower-paced contrast to the daytime safaris, with sightings never guaranteed. Warm clothing is worth having, since temperatures drop quickly after sunset.

brazil/bonito-town.name: Bonito town centre
brazil/bonito-town.description: A small, orderly town in Mato Grosso do Sul built around the tour operators who run the surrounding rivers and caves.
brazil/bonito-town.details: Bonito grew around tourism to the clear rivers and caves in the surrounding countryside, and most of its main street is given over to tour agencies, outdoor shops and restaurants rather than historic sights of its own. Nearly all the actual attractions, including the rivers and caves, are a drive outside town and run on a permit system that controls daily visitor numbers. The town itself makes an easy, low-key base between outings. It is flat and simple to get around on foot.

brazil/rio-da-prata.name: Snorkelling at Rio da Prata
brazil/rio-da-prata.description: A long float downstream through an exceptionally clear, fish-filled river near Bonito, done in a wetsuit and snorkel mask.
brazil/rio-da-prata.details: The river's water is filtered through limestone before reaching the surface, which is what gives it its unusual clarity and lets snorkellers see fish clearly from above rather than just below. Visitors walk a short path to the river, then float downstream with the current for an extended stretch, led by a guide. Wetsuits are provided and worth using, since the water stays cool year-round. Visitor numbers are capped and controlled by permit, so access runs through a licensed operator rather than independently.

brazil/gruta-lago-azul.name: Gruta do Lago Azul (Blue Lake Cave)
brazil/gruta-lago-azul.description: A limestone cave near Bonito holding a brilliant blue underground lake, reached down a long staircase.
brazil/gruta-lago-azul.details: A steep staircase descends into the cave's single large chamber, at the bottom of which sits a lake whose water appears a striking blue under certain light conditions, caused by dissolved limestone and the angle of sunlight entering the cave mouth. The effect is strongest around midday, when the sun reaches furthest into the chamber. The lake itself is deep and swimming is not permitted, so the visit is a viewing rather than a swimming stop. Entry is timed and limited by permit, as with most sites around Bonito.

brazil/dois-irmaos-hike.name: Dois Irmãos viewpoint hike
brazil/dois-irmaos-hike.description: A forested trail above Rio's Vidigal neighbourhood, ending at a viewpoint over the beaches and hills of the coastline.
brazil/dois-irmaos-hike.details: The trail climbs through forest above Vidigal, one of the hillside neighbourhoods overlooking São Conrado and Leblon, ending below the twin peaks known as Dois Irmãos with a wide view along the coast. It is steep in places and takes a couple of hours round trip at a steady pace. Guided options are available and generally preferred, since the trail passes close to the edge of the neighbourhood above. The payoff is one of the better coastal views in the city, without the crowds of Sugarloaf or Corcovado.

brazil/samba-school-rehearsal.name: Samba school rehearsal night
brazil/samba-school-rehearsal.description: An open rehearsal night at one of Rio's samba schools, with live drumming and dancing outside the Carnival season.
brazil/samba-school-rehearsal.details: Samba schools are community organisations that spend much of the year preparing the music, costumes and choreography for their Carnival parade entry, and many open their rehearsal nights to visitors for a fee. The atmosphere is informal and participatory rather than a staged show, with a live drum section and dancers of all levels on the floor. Rehearsals typically run late into the night. It gives a more local view of Carnival culture than a daytime museum visit.

brazil/churrascaria-dinner.name: Farewell churrascaria dinner
brazil/churrascaria-dinner.description: A Brazilian steakhouse dinner, with servers carving a continuous rotation of grilled meats directly at the table.

brazil/teatro-amazonas.name: Teatro Amazonas
brazil/teatro-amazonas.description: An ornate opera house in the centre of Manaus, built during the Amazon rubber boom of the late 19th century.
brazil/teatro-amazonas.details: Teatro Amazonas was built when Manaus grew wealthy on the rubber trade, and its domed exterior, tiled in the colours of the Brazilian flag, and richly decorated interior reflect that brief period of prosperity. It remains in use for concerts and still hosts a seasonal opera festival. Guided tours usually cover the auditorium, foyer and a few of the painted ceilings when the theatre is not in use for a performance or rehearsal. Check ahead for interior visiting hours, since they vary around the theatre's own schedule.

brazil/meeting-of-waters.name: Meeting of the Waters
brazil/meeting-of-waters.description: The point near Manaus where the dark Rio Negro and the paler, sediment-rich Rio Solimões run side by side before mixing into the Amazon proper.
brazil/meeting-of-waters.details: The two rivers differ in colour, temperature and speed, so for several kilometres downstream of their confluence they flow side by side in visibly distinct bands rather than blending immediately. The effect is usually seen from a boat on the way to or from a lodge rather than as a separate excursion. Which river feeds the main channel of the Amazon from this point on is a point of ongoing local debate rather than settled fact. The view is best in clear conditions, since overcast light flattens the colour contrast.

brazil/amazon-sunset-canoe.name: Sunset canoe paddle near the lodge
brazil/amazon-sunset-canoe.description: A quiet canoe outing on flooded forest channels close to an Amazon jungle lodge, timed for sunset.

brazil/amazon-jungle-trek.name: Guided rainforest trek
brazil/amazon-jungle-trek.description: A guided walk through Amazon rainforest near a jungle lodge, with a naturalist pointing out tracks, calls and plants.
brazil/amazon-jungle-trek.details: A local guide leads the walk along forest trails near the lodge, identifying animal tracks, calls and the medicinal or practical uses of plants along the way. Sightings of larger animals are not guaranteed, since much of the forest's wildlife is shy or active mainly at night, but insects, birds and smaller creatures are reliably seen. The ground is uneven, often damp, and can have exposed roots, so sturdy closed footwear matters. Insect repellent and long sleeves are worth wearing regardless of the season.

brazil/amazon-caiman-spotting.name: Night caiman-spotting boat trip
brazil/amazon-caiman-spotting.description: An after-dark boat trip along quiet Amazon channels, using a spotlight to find caimans resting at the water's edge.
brazil/amazon-caiman-spotting.details: A guide steers slowly along narrow channels after dark, sweeping a handheld spotlight along the banks to catch the red eyeshine of caimans resting near the water. Frogs, nightjars and other nocturnal sounds are usually more noticeable than anything seen clearly. The boat is generally a small, low craft rather than anything motorised and fast. Warm, dark clothing helps avoid both insects and the evening chill on the water.

brazil/amazon-piranha-fishing.name: Piranha fishing on a blackwater tributary
brazil/amazon-piranha-fishing.description: A guided fishing outing on a quiet Amazon tributary, with a guide handling hooks and releasing the catch.
brazil/amazon-piranha-fishing.details: Blackwater tributaries, stained dark by decomposing plant matter, are a common setting for a short piranha-fishing outing from a jungle lodge, usually done from a small boat with simple hand lines. A guide baits and removes hooks throughout, and fish are generally released rather than kept. The activity is as much about seeing the river up close as it is about the fishing itself. Sun protection is worth having, since there is little shade on the water.

brazil.name: Brazil
brazil.description: A continent-sized country of rainforest, wetlands, waterfalls and a long Atlantic coastline, with samba, football and Carnival at the centre of its culture.

brazil/rio-de-janeiro.name: Rio de Janeiro
brazil/rio-de-janeiro.description: A beachfront city wedged between forested granite peaks and the sea, known for Christ the Redeemer, Sugarloaf Mountain and the beaches of Copacabana and Ipanema.

brazil/sao-paulo.name: São Paulo
brazil/sao-paulo.description: Brazil's largest city, a sprawling business and cultural hub known for its food scene, museums and street art rather than postcard sights.

brazil/parana.name: Paraná
brazil/parana.description: A southern Brazilian state on the border with Argentina and Paraguay, home to the Brazilian side of the Iguazu Falls.

brazil/foz-do-iguacu.name: Foz do Iguaçu
brazil/foz-do-iguacu.description: A border town built around the Brazilian approach to the Iguazu Falls, where the Iguaçu River drops over a wide curve of cliffs.

brazil/bahia.name: Bahia
brazil/bahia.description: A northeastern coastal state settled early in Brazil's colonial era, with a strong Afro-Brazilian culture expressed through food, music and religion.

brazil/salvador.name: Salvador
brazil/salvador.description: Bahia's capital and one of the Americas' oldest cities, known for the colonial old town of Pelourinho and its Afro-Brazilian culture.

brazil/mato-grosso-do-sul.name: Mato Grosso do Sul
brazil/mato-grosso-do-sul.description: A central-western state covering part of the Pantanal wetland and the clear rivers and caves around Bonito.

brazil/pantanal.name: Pantanal
brazil/pantanal.description: The world's largest tropical wetland, flooding seasonally across central-western Brazil and known for dense concentrations of wildlife.

brazil/bonito.name: Bonito
brazil/bonito.description: A small town in Mato Grosso do Sul known for exceptionally clear rivers, caves and controlled-access nature sites built around them.

brazil/amazonas.name: Amazonas
brazil/amazonas.description: Brazil's largest state, almost entirely covered by Amazon rainforest and reached mainly by river and air from its capital, Manaus.

brazil/manaus.name: Manaus
brazil/manaus.description: A city deep in the Amazon rainforest on the Rio Negro, used as the usual gateway for river trips and jungle lodges.
